name: Golden Bridge
label: Golden Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chùa Linh Ứng' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Chùa Linh Ứng' (way/746227054): middle (31 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/683416736: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Golden Bridge' (119 m long).
notes: Famous footbridge held by giant stone hands at Ba Na Hills.

text.description:
The Golden Bridge (Cầu Vàng) is a pedestrian walkway in the Bà Nà Hills resort, in Hòa Vang district. It is about 150 metres long and curves almost back on itself. Two giant hands, built from fibreglass and wire mesh to look like stone, seem to hold it up. It was built to link the cable car station with the gardens, and it also works as a lookout. Construction began in July 2017 and finished in April 2018, and the bridge opened in June 2018.

The best-known photos are taken on the bridge, but this map's stand-here point is at Chùa Linh Ứng, in the pagoda grounds near the bridge area. From here you see the whole bridge from a distance, across the valley, with mountains and prayer flags in the scene. It is also usually quieter than the bridge, and one visitor found it nearly empty during a 30-minute stay.

The bridge looks small from this far away, so use your phone's zoom lens and let the valley and the flags give the picture scale. Fog often covers the view, so a clear day makes a big difference. If you want a close, upward shot of the stone hands, Cầu Vàng itself gives that view, and Le Jardin D'Amour shows the bridge arching overhead.
text.geographic_location: The bridge is in the Bà Nà Hills resort in Hòa Vang district, Da Nang, and joins the cable car station to the gardens.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so make your way from central Da Nang to Sun World Ba Na Hills. In Google Maps you may need to search for "Sun World Ba Na Hills" rather than the bridge name. Once inside, the bridge is reached only by cable car. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) to bring the bridge closer across the valley. The default lens (1x) is better for the wider scene with the mountains and prayer flags. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a flag or the pagoda grounds large in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Chùa Linh Ứng (pagoda grounds near the Golden Bridge area). The bridge seen from a distance across the valley, with mountains and prayer flags in the scene. From there the bridge lies to the south-east, seen from a distance across the valley, with mountains and prayer flags around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the bridge on one of the lines, not in the centre. Let prayer flags or the valley fill the foreground so the bridge has some scale. Take one wide shot at 1x, then a closer one with the telephoto. For a different angle, Le Jardin D'Amour has the bridge arching overhead with the stone hands and flower beds in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. If mist drifts through, take a few shots a minute apart. A panorama can capture the whole valley, but hold the phone steady while it sweeps. Drones are not permitted.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go on a clear day and take the first cable car, around 7:00 to 8:00 AM, because fog often covers the view later. Check opening hours and any closures before your visit.

text.access_note: This is inside the Sun World Ba Na Hills park, so an entry ticket is needed; check the official site before you go for tickets, hours and closures.

name: Marble Mountains
label: Marble Mountains
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Vọng Giang Đài' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Vong Giang Dai' (node/5922491411): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8552348: large area 'Marble Mountains' (1440 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Five limestone hills with caves, pagodas and viewpoints.

text.description:
The Marble Mountains, also called Ngũ Hành Sơn or 'five elements mountains', are a cluster of five marble and limestone hills just south of Da Nang city. Each hill is named after an element: metal, water, wood, fire and earth. They rise sharply out of flat land close to the coast, so they stand out in any wide view. Thủy Sơn is the one visitors can climb. Its 156 steps lead to a summit with wide views, and its caves and Buddhist and Hindu shrines hold carved statues and reliefs.

The best-known photo is taken from Vọng Giang Đài, a stone pavilion on the west side of Thủy Sơn. From the pavilion you look back over all five hills together, with Non Nuoc Beach, the Co Co River and the Da Nang skyline behind them. Guides treat it as the main viewpoint, and it is the one place where all five hills fit into a single frame.

The area is also known for stone carving, and the mountains were given National Special Relic status in January 2019. If you have time, two other spots are worth a look. Động Huyền Không is a cave where a shaft of daylight falls through the roof onto the altar and statues. The highest point, Đỉnh Thượng Thái, looks east over the coast. Take the pavilion photo first, while the light is soft, then explore the caves.
text.geographic_location: The Marble Mountains are in Ngũ Hành Sơn District, south of Da Nang city, near Non Nuoc Beach. The five hills stand together as a small cluster of rock. The Co Co River is visible behind them in the view from the pavilion.
text.directions_text: From central Da Nang, head south towards Ngũ Hành Sơn District by taxi or hired scooter. Ask for Thủy Sơn and Tam Thai Pagoda. From the pagoda, climb the steps up the west side of Thủy Sơn to Vọng Giang Đài. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the pavilion, so all five hills and the skyline fit in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single hill or the beach.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Vọng Giang Đài (west side of Thủy Sơn, reached by the steps from Tam Thai Pagoda). From the stone pavilion you look back over the five marble hills together, with Non Nuoc Beach, the Co Co River and the Da Nang skyline behind them. The stone pavilion on the west side of Thủy Sơn, reached by the steps from Tam Thai Pagoda. From the pavilion you look back over the five marble hills, with Non Nuoc Beach, the Co Co River and the Da Nang skyline behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line of hills on the lower third, so the sky and skyline fill the rest. Include a corner of the pavilion's stone edge in the foreground to add depth. If you go on to Động Huyền Không, shoot the beam of light falling on the altar and statues, with the incense smoke in it. Hold the phone steady and ask before photographing monks or altars.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hills to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. In the dim cave, tap on the lit altar and lower the exposure so the beam doesn't blow out. Night mode may kick in in dark corners, so keep your hands still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset, when the light is warm and soft. Check the official site before you go, as the site closes in the late afternoon and sunset may fall after closing.

text.access_note: This is a visited religious and heritage site with pagodas and shrines, and parts of it may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: My Khe Beach
label: My Khe Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Võ Nguyên Giáp' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Võ Nguyên Giáp nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM R19000664 (My Khe Beach): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Long city beach with sunrise views.

text.description: My Khe is a long city beach in Da Nang, and it works well for phone photos because the scene is simple: sand, sea and a wide sky. The best frame is at sunrise. The light is low and golden on the wet sand, and basket boats and fishermen are often on the shore with the open sea behind them. A local photography guide describes sunrise as the one-hour window for shooting My Khe. The stretch in front of Võ Nguyên Giáp street is said to be less crowded than the hotel section further north. If you want a different kind of picture, the palm-lined pavements along the same street make good frames for portraits of your travelling companions. Aim to arrive a little before the light changes, so you have time to walk down to the sand and look for a boat or a figure to give the picture a focus. One guide says the beach is busier in the late afternoon, so early morning gives you the calmest scene. Keep an eye on the flags, as rip currents occur here, and stay out of the water while you are concentrating on your screen.
text.geographic_location: My Khe Beach is a city beach in Da Nang with the open sea beyond the shore, and Son Tra Peninsula is visible in the distance. The stretch for this photo lies in front of Võ Nguyên Giáp street, near the Fusion Maia resort entrance.
text.directions_text: There are no public transport stops at this spot; get to Võ Nguyên Giáp street, near the Fusion Maia resort entrance, by your own means. Then walk onto the beach in front of the street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the boats, the wet sand and the sea. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of the shore. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a fisherman or a single boat.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Võ Nguyên Giáp (beach stretch in front of the street, near the Fusion Maia resort entrance). Low, golden sunrise light on wet sand, with basket boats and fishermen on the shore and the open sea beyond. Near the Fusion Maia resort entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower line so it stays level. Keep a boat or fisherman in the foreground to give the scene scale. For portraits, try portrait mode against the palm-lined pavements along the street. As an alternative, from the beach itself (Bãi biển Mỹ Khê), Son Tra Peninsula rises in the distance with the Lady Buddha statue visible on the mountain, and Công viên Biển Đông has the carp-turned-dragon statue against the sea.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunrise colours stay rich. Use night mode only if it is still quite dark, and hold the phone steady against your body. Take a Live Photo to catch boats moving on the shore.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: About 5:45 AM from November to March, before the boats leave around 6:30 AM.

text.access_note: This is a stretch of public beach with no payment needed; mind the warning flags because of rip currents, and check local rules before flying a drone.

name: Dragon Bridge
label: Dragon Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bạch Đằng' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Bạch Đằng nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/694831926: large area 'Dragon Bridge' (763 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Fire-breathing steel dragon bridge over the Hàn River, best at night.

text.description:
The Dragon Bridge (Cầu Rồng) carries traffic across the Han River in the shape of a steel dragon, and it is easy to see why people photograph it. Its long, curving body is the sort of shape that suits a phone's wide view. It is described as the world's largest dragon-shaped steel bridge. It is 666 m long and 37.5 m wide, with six traffic lanes. The main span was finished in October 2012, and the bridge opened to traffic on 29 March 2013.

The best view for a relaxed, wide shot is from the riverside promenade on Bạch Đằng, on the city-centre bank. From there you can see the whole bridge side-on across the water, with the city skyline and river reflections behind it. There is more room here, and less spray, than right under the dragon's head.

The bridge is also known for a fire and water show on weekend nights, listed as Saturday and Sunday at 9 pm. It may run on Fridays too, so check the current schedule locally. On other nights you should only expect the lighting. If you want a close, front-on shot of the head during the show, Trần Hưng Đạo is the alternative. Keep clear of the bridge deck and the dragon's mouth, as some visitors report spray and the deck is closed to traffic shortly before the show.
text.geographic_location: The Dragon Bridge crosses the Han River in central Da Nang, at the Le Dinh Duong/Bach Dang traffic circle, on the route between the airport and My Khe Beach. This viewpoint is on the riverside promenade on the city-centre (west) bank.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Da Nang, go by taxi or hired scooter to the riverside street Bạch Đằng on the west bank and walk to the promenade edge facing the bridge. Check the orientation on the map, as the east and west banks are described differently in different guides. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole bridge and the skyline into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the dragon's head and the lights on the span.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bạch Đằng (west (city-centre) bank, riverside promenade, facing the bridge's profile). The whole bridge in side profile across the Han River, with the city skyline and river reflections behind it. From here you see the whole bridge in side profile across the Han River, with the city skyline and river reflections behind it. For a closer, front-on view of the dragon's head during the show, Trần Hưng Đạo is the alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the bridge along the lower third, so the sky and the reflections get space. Include some of the water in the foreground so the bridge's lights have something to reflect in. Keep the phone level so the long span does not look tilted. An alternative angle is Cầu Trần Thị Lý, which gives a side-on view of the whole bridge in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the lights do not burn out against the dark sky. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone as still as you can, with your elbows tucked in. Take a few frames in case of movement. A Live Photo can catch the flames during the show, but video is better for movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around dusk and into the evening, when the bridge is lit and the reflections show up on the water. For the fire and water show, arrive early on a weekend night, before the 9 pm start, to get a good place on the promenade.

text.access_note: The bridge deck is closed to traffic shortly before the weekend show, so check locally for current show times before you go.

name: Han Market
label: Han Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nguyễn Thái Học' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Nguyễn Thái Học nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W204885903 (Han Market): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Busy central market by the river.

text.description:
Han Market is a busy everyday market in central Da Nang, and the most characterful way to photograph it is from the side rather than the front. The narrow lane of Nguyễn Thái Học runs alongside the market's side wall. Here you get ordinary street life: small drink stalls, hair-salon shopfronts and a slightly older, less polished look. The lane has an old-fashioned feel that changes little, which makes it a good alternative to the crowded main entrance.

The pictures work because of the layers: the textured side wall, the drink stalls, the hair-salon shopfronts and passers-by. Start with a wide shot of the lane to show where you are, then move in on details such as a stall, a cup or a doorway. If you want the classic view, the market's front entrance has its signage and the flow of shoppers framed by the street. Access to the main Trần Phú-side entrance is not always open, and one guide says a side door on Yên Bái street may be needed instead. Check on the day which street bounds the market's fourth side, and rely on the market wall itself and the map. Ask vendors before taking close-up shots of them or their goods, and keep to the edge of the lane so you do not block people.
text.geographic_location: Han Market is in central Da Nang, with Trần Phú street on its main-entrance side and Yên Bái street on another. The Dragon Bridge is about 950 m away.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stops are listed for this spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lane and the side wall as people see it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the lane feels too tight to fit the wall and the shopfronts in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as a drink stall or signs, so you can stay back from vendors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Nguyễn Thái Học (Narrow lane running alongside the market's side wall). Everyday street life and the market's side wall, with small drink stalls and hair-salon shopfronts that give an older, less polished look. From here the photo shows everyday street life, the market's side wall, and the small drink stalls and hair-salon shopfronts along the lane.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use them to keep the wall and doorways upright. Place a stall or a passing person on one third of the frame and let the wall fill the rest. For an alternative, walk round to the market's front entrance to photograph the signage with shoppers passing through, framed by the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stall or wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if bright sky or shopfronts wash out the highlights. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of people in the lane, and ask before photographing vendors up close.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No specific best time is known for this spot, so visit whenever suits you.

text.access_note: The market is a working public market, and the main Trần Phú-side entrance is not always open (a side door on Yên Bái street may be needed), so ask vendors before close-up shots.

name: Linh Ung Pagoda
label: Linh Ung Pagoda
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chùa Linh Ứng Bãi Bụt' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W746227054 (Linh Ung Pagoda): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Pagoda on Son Tra with the 67 m Lady Buddha statue.

text.description:
Linh Ung Pagoda is a working Buddhist complex on the coast, best known for the 67 m Lady Buddha statue that stands over the sea. It is a good place for phone photos because the statue, the East Sea, Da Nang Bay and the forested hillside all line up in one frame, with plenty of room to move around for different angles.

The best-regarded photo area is the upper terrace around the statue's lotus base. The far right (east) side of that terrace lets you shoot across the statue towards the open sea, so she fills the foreground and the bay and coastline fill the background. If you want a different picture, the layered entrance gate, Cổng Tam Quan, frames the statue above it, with the bay and My Khe Beach seen through the arch. Xa Loi Tower, a multi-storey relic tower, has the ocean behind it and is often quieter.

This is a place of worship, so photograph with respect. Photography inside the prayer halls is often restricted, so look for signs. Avoid flash, and don't stand in front of shrines or block pathways for a shot. The statue's exact coordinates differ between map pages, so check the phone icon on the map before you start walking. Go in the morning if you can, when the light is soft.
text.geographic_location: Linh Ung Pagoda (Chùa Linh Ứng Bãi Bụt) is on the coast of Da Nang, looking out over the East Sea and Da Nang Bay.
text.directions_text: There are no rail or tram stops nearby. Set the phone icon on the map as your destination, as it marks the pagoda. Once you arrive, follow the paths up through the complex towards the statue's base. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main shot of the statue with the sea behind. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to the base and want the whole statue and the lotus terrace in one frame. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the gate, Xa Loi Tower or the coastline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Once there, head for the upper terrace at the Lady Buddha's lotus base and stand at the far right (east) side, shooting across the statue towards the open sea. The statue is in the foreground with the East Sea and Da Nang Bay behind her.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on one of the vertical lines, leaving the sea and coastline in the rest of the frame. Keep the horizon level. For a second picture, try the Cổng Tam Quan gate, which frames the statue above it with the bay and My Khe Beach through the arch. Xa Loi Tower is another option, with the ocean behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out the sea and the statue's detail. Take a few frames in case someone walks through, and wipe the lens first as sea air can leave a haze.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the light is soft and before direct sun reaches the statue.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship, so follow the signs about photography, and check the official site for current opening hours and any entry rules before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Sea air can leave a haze on a phone lens.

name: Museum of Cham Sculpture
label: Cham Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/302872188: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Đà Nẵng Museum of Cham Sculpture' (184 m across).
notes: Largest collection of Cham sculpture in the world.

text.description: The Museum of Cham Sculpture is in Hải Châu District, close to the Han River. It holds what is described as the world's largest collection of Cham sculpture, so it is a good place to photograph carved stone figures, reliefs and altars from the Cham culture of central Vietnam. The first building opened in 1919. It was designed by two French architects, who were encouraged by the archaeologist Henri Parmentier to bring traditional Cham elements into the design. The museum was extended in the mid-1930s and again in 2002, so you are looking at several layers of building rather than one. That mix makes the outside worth a few frames before you go in. The carvings themselves reward close attention. The carved figures and reliefs have strong textures, and a phone picks these up well if you move in close and keep the camera steady. Start with one wide shot of the building or its grounds to set the scene. Then switch to details: a face, a hand, a pattern along an edge. Look for a plain background behind each piece, such as a bare wall, so the carving stands out. Rooms can be dim and glass or labels can reflect, so step slightly to one side and watch for your own shadow. Photography rules inside may differ from room to room, so follow any signs and ask staff if unsure.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in Hải Châu District in central Da Nang, near the Han River.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so start from central Hải Châu District near the Han River. Go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Museum of Cham Sculpture (Bảo tàng Điêu khắc Chăm). The phone icon on the map is at the museum, so once you arrive you are already at the starting position for your photos. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the building and its grounds, and the default lens (1x) for most other shots. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved details without leaning over displays.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Move around the grounds to find a spot with a clear view of the exterior, then step back far enough to fit the whole front in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the building's vertical lines straight to avoid a leaning look. For sculptures indoors, fill the frame with one piece and keep the background plain. Portrait mode can help a statue stand out, but check the edges look natural.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the carving to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so pale stone does not turn washed-out. In dim galleries, hold the phone steady against your body or a solid surface and let night mode work if it switches on. Avoid using flash.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: For the outside of the building, morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. Indoors the light is fairly similar all day, so choose a time when the galleries are quieter.

text.access_note: This is a museum and is likely to be ticketed with set opening hours and photography rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: Hàn River Bridge
label: Han River Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bạch Đằng' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Bạch Đằng nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Hàn River Bridge'.
notes: Swing bridge that rotates at night.

text.description:
The Hàn River Bridge is the cable-stayed swing bridge that links the west bank of Da Nang with the east side, where the beaches are. It opened on 29 March 2000 and is the only swing bridge still operating in Vietnam. Its swing span is 122.7 metres long and turns on a round pier in the middle of the river. It appears on the city's logo, so it makes a good 'I was in Da Nang' photo.

It photographs best from the west-bank riverside promenade on Bạch Đằng. From there you look straight across the water at the bridge, with the city skyline and the river reflections behind it. The view is wide and clear, and it gets better once the bridge and waterfront are lit after sunset. Avoid the bridge deck itself: it is a poor place to photograph the bridge.

If you stay late, the bridge swings open for passing boats. At weekends this is at 11 pm, with traffic stopped from 10:45 pm and about 15 minutes for the span to turn. Weekday and late-night times vary, so check locally and arrive 20 to 30 minutes early. On weekend evenings the promenades also fill up for the nearby Dragon Bridge fire show, so claim your spot early. For a different angle, try Trần Hưng Đạo for a river-level view of the bridge and city lights, or the east end on Phạm Văn Đồng, with the sea behind the bridge.
text.geographic_location: The bridge is in downtown Da Nang, crossing the Hàn River between Lê Duẩn Street on the west bank and Phạm Văn Đồng Street on the east bank.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or train stops nearby, so head for the west bank of the Hàn River in central Da Nang by taxi or hired scooter. Ask to be dropped on the Bạch Đằng riverside promenade, near the western end of the Hàn River Bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the bridge, the river and the skyline together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the tower and cables, or lit details on the far bank.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bạch Đằng (west bank riverside promenade, facing the bridge across the Han River). A wide, unobstructed view across the river to the swing bridge, with the city skyline and river reflections in frame. On the west-bank riverside promenade, facing east across the Hàn River to the swing bridge. From here you get a wide, clear view of the bridge with the city skyline and the reflections on the water in frame. Guides suggest the best blue-hour spot is on the promenade between the Hàn River Bridge and the Dragon Bridge, facing southeast.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the bridge along a lower third line, leaving room for the sky and the reflections in the water. Keep the horizon level. If you want a different view, try Trần Hưng Đạo for a river-level shot, or the east end on Phạm Văn Đồng with the sea behind the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a solid surface or lean against a wall to keep the phone steady. Tap the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights do not wash out. Live Photos can catch passing boats and moving reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour is the best time, with the sky still blue and the bridge lights on. Guides suggest about 6:00-6:30 PM in winter and 6:30-7:00 PM in summer. If you want to see the bridge swing open, check the current timing locally and arrive 20 to 30 minutes early.

text.access_note: The promenade viewpoint is an open public space with no ticket needed, but check locally for the bridge's swing times and any temporary closures.

name: Son Tra Mountain
label: Son Tra Mountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ban Co Peak' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ban Co Peak' (node/1538334281): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1623183649: the OpenStreetMap point 'Son Tra Mountain'.
notes: Forested peninsula with coastal viewpoints and langurs.

text.description: Sơn Trà Mountain, also called Monkey Mountain, is the forested ridge of the Sơn Trà Peninsula, which juts out into the East Sea beside Da Nang Bay. Most of its photo value comes from what you see from the top. Ban Co Peak, the peninsula's highest point at nearly 600 m, is the viewpoint at the summit area. From the summit the bay, My Khe Beach and the whole city lie spread out below, with dark green slopes filling the foreground. Guides call it the broadest panorama on the peninsula, and sunrise is picked out as the best time. The summit is a short walk from the road. Ban Co means Chessboard, and a chessboard stone is at the top. The mountain has been a nature reserve since 1992, covering about 26 square kilometres. It is home to the red-shanked douc langur, so you may see wildlife as well as views. On a clear day you can also pick out Hai Van Pass, Lien Chieu Bay, Ba Na Hills and the Cham Islands. If you want a different angle, Linh Ứng Pagoda puts the 67-metre Lady Buddha in the foreground with the bay beyond. Thuận Phước Bridge looks back towards the green mountains of Sơn Trà. Keep to public areas: the radar station area is military, and photography there may be restricted.
text.geographic_location: Sơn Trà Mountain is on the Sơn Trà Peninsula in Sơn Trà district, Da Nang, overlooking Da Nang Bay and the East Sea. Tiên Sa port sits at the foot of its western face.
text.directions_text: From central Da Nang, head for the Sơn Trà Peninsula and then Ban Co Peak. The roads up the mountain are steep and narrow, and scooters are not allowed on the mountain routes, so do not plan on hiring one. The last stretch to the summit area is a short walk from the road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bay and city. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the forested slopes in the foreground. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out My Khe Beach or a single stretch of coastline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (summit area of the peninsula's highest ridge; the chessboard stone is at the top). Da Nang Bay, My Khe Beach and the city stretching below, with the peninsula's forested slopes in the foreground. Ban Co Peak is the recommended summit viewpoint, close to the chessboard stone at the top. From the summit you look out over Da Nang Bay, My Khe Beach and the city below, with the peninsula's forested slopes in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper third line so the bay and city fill most of the frame. Keep a patch of green slope in the bottom corner to give depth. For the full sweep of the bay, try panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone level. If you also want the Lady Buddha, Linh Ứng Pagoda is a good second stop, and Thuận Phước Bridge works as a view back towards the mountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the city to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. If you see langurs, use the telephoto from a distance and do not approach or feed them.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise, which guides single out as the best moment on the peak.

text.access_note: Ban Co Peak is described as free to visit, but access rules can change and the radar station area is military, so check current access rules locally before you go.

name: Da Nang Cathedral
label: Da Nang Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Trần Phú' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Trần Phú nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM W404714309 (Da Nang Cathedral): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Pink French-era Catholic church topped with a rooster weathervane.

text.description:
Da Nang Cathedral is easy to spot in the city centre: a pink church with a tall spire and a bell tower topped with a rooster. That colour is what makes it work so well on a phone. The pink stands out against a blue sky and the palm trees nearby, so even a quick snap looks cheerful and clear.

The classic shot is straight-on from the opposite side of Trần Phú, directly across from the front gate. From there the whole facade, the spire and the rooster tower fit into one frame, with palm trees at the edges. If you can get into the grounds, there are two other pictures. One is a diagonal view of the bell tower and roof framed by the gateway, which makes the building look taller. The other is a quieter scene with the Lourdes-style grotto and religious statues in the foreground.

A few practical points. The gates are locked during Mass, at lunch and sometimes on Sundays, so the courtyard and grotto may be out of reach then. A back gate is sometimes open when the main one is shut. Photography inside is not allowed during services. Renovation work may block some angles, so check what you can see when you arrive. The road in front is busy, so take your photo from the pavement and never step into the traffic to get the whole building in.
text.geographic_location: In central Da Nang, on Trần Phú street, facing the road with its front gate.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stop is listed for this spot, so from central Da Nang come by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Da Nang Cathedral on Trần Phú. From there the cathedral is to the west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the road, which fits the facade, spire and tower together. If traffic or railings stop you stepping back far enough, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use 2x or more to pick out the rooster on top of the bell tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Trần Phú (opposite side of the street, straight across from the front gate). The full pink facade, spire and rooster-topped bell tower, with palm trees and blue sky in the frame. On the opposite side of the street, straight across from the front gate. From here the cathedral is to the west, and you see the full pink facade, spire and rooster-topped bell tower with palm trees and blue sky around them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the spire up with the centre of the screen, so the tower stands upright. Keep the palm trees at the edges as a natural frame. If the gates are open, an alternative is the diagonal view of the bell tower through the gateway, or the grotto and statues in the foreground of the courtyard.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pink facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky stays blue and the walls don't wash out. Stay on the pavement, and wait for a gap in the traffic rather than leaning into the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 9 a.m., when the light is soft and there are fewer people about.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a place of worship and its gates are locked at times such as Mass and lunch, so check the current opening hours before you go; the Trần Phú viewpoint itself is on a public street.

name: Love Lock Bridge
label: Love Lock Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Tượng Cá Chép Hóa Rồng' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Ca Chep Hoa Rong' (pois); moved 20 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OSM N5072875821 (Love Bridge): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Riverside bridge covered in love padlocks, next to the Dragon Bridge.

text.description:
Love Lock Bridge has padlocked railings and rows of heart-shaped lanterns along the river. The best phone photo here starts at the statue, not on the bridge. Tượng Cá Chép Hóa Rồng, the carp-turned-dragon sculpture, is where the map's stand-here point is placed, on Trần Hưng Đạo. Check on the day. Get low beside the base of the statue and shoot upward. The sculpture then looks tall and dramatic against the sky, which gives you a strong foreground and a clear sense of place in one frame.

Once you have the statue shot, head to the bridge itself for a second picture. The heart lanterns and padlocked railings make a good repeating pattern. The river is beside you, and Dragon Bridge shows in the distance. Both pictures work best under a blue sky or at sunset. Sunset is usually given as roughly 5:30 to 6:30 p.m., but check the time on the day. Dragon Bridge's fire-and-water show is reported for 9 p.m. at weekends, and the area gets crowded then. If you want a clean shot of the statue, go earlier. Wait for a gap between passers-by rather than rushing, and keep your phone steady against your body or a railing.
text.geographic_location: Dragon Bridge is visible further along the river.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the statue, so you fit its full height and some of its surroundings into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the lantern rows and railings. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it from the bridge to compress the padlocks and lanterns into a tight pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (base of the statue at the bridgehead, on the riverbank beside the bridge). The tall carp-turned-dragon sculpture in the foreground with the bridge curving behind it, shot upward against the sky. Kneel or stand low next to the statue and aim your phone upward, with the tall sculpture in the foreground and the sky behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the statue large in the frame and use the gridlines to keep it upright. Shooting up from low down makes the sculpture look dramatic. For a second picture, go to Cầu Tình Yêu itself and shoot along the heart-lantern rows and padlocked railings, with the river and Dragon Bridge in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so a bright sky stays blue and the sculpture keeps its detail. After dark, turn on night mode and hold your elbows against your body for steadiness.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: When the sky is blue, or at sunset (roughly 5:30 to 6:30 p.m., but check the time on the day). Expect crowds on weekend evenings around Dragon Bridge's 9 p.m. show.

text.access_note: This looks like an open public riverside space, but check locally before you go in case of any restrictions.

name: Trần Thị Lý Bridge
label: Tran Thi Ly Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bạch Đằng' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Bạch Đằng nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/160628034: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Tran Thi Ly Bridge' (756 m long).
notes: Sail-shaped cable-stayed bridge over the Hàn River.

text.description:
The Nguyễn Văn Trỗi–Trần Thị Lý Bridge, usually just called Trần Thị Lý Bridge, is a cable-stayed bridge over the Hàn River. Its leaning tower and fan of sail-like cables make a strong shape against the sky, and from the riverbank the whole span sits neatly in one frame. The best photo here is a wider view, with the bridge, its reflection in the water, the city skyline and the neighbouring bridges all together.

The bridge opened on 29 March 2013 and is 731 metres long and 145 metres tall. It replaced two older bridges and stands where Da Nang's first bridge was built in 1951. That bridge has carried several names since, including Trần Thị Lý from 1975.

For the best result, walk the riverside stretch of Bạch Đằng and stand back far enough to fit the tower and its reflection in. Keep your phone level so the deck doesn't slope, and wait for a gap in the people walking past. If you want the full height of the tower without vehicles in the foreground, Cầu Nguyễn Văn Trỗi is a good alternative. Trần Hưng Đạo gives a quieter, lower view across the water. Take your photos from the bank, not the traffic deck, as the road is busy.
text.geographic_location: The bridge crosses the Hàn River in central Da Nang and links Hải Châu, Sơn Trà and Ngũ Hành Sơn districts. The viewpoint is on the riverside street Bạch Đằng, close to the bridge.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stop is near this spot, so start from the central riverside area of Da Nang and take a taxi or hired scooter to Bạch Đằng, on the Hàn River bank near the bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the bridge, its reflection and the skyline in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the tower and cables. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the cables fanning out from the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bạch Đằng (riverside stretch along the Han River bank, near the bridge). A wider view of the bridge and its reflection in the river, with the city skyline and neighbouring bridges in the same frame. The bridge lies to the east of you. From here you can see the bridge and its reflection in the river, with the city skyline and neighbouring bridges in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the bridge deck up with a horizontal line so it doesn't tilt. Keep some water in the lower part of the frame so the reflection is part of the picture. If you want the full height of the leaning tower with no traffic in front, try Cầu Nguyễn Văn Trỗi. For a quieter, lower view across the water, try Trần Hưng Đạo.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights don't wash out. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a railing to keep the phone steady. Hold still until the shot finishes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the bridge's LED lights come on and the reflections are strongest.

text.access_note: Bạch Đằng is an open public street with riverside walkways, but take your photos from the bank rather than the traffic deck, and check local signs before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Bạch Đằng runs along the Hàn River bank on the western side of the bridge, which is why the bridge appears to the east.
The riverside walkway is a public area and can be reached without a ticket.
The telephoto lens (2x-5x) can pick out cable details, and the ultra-wide (0.5x) can fit the bridge, reflection and skyline in one frame.
The riverside walkway may be busier with walkers in the evening.

name: Thuận Phước Bridge
label: Thuan Phuoc Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Đường Như Nguyệt' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Đường Như Nguyệt' (way/344533399): point nearest the subject (1442 m long).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Long suspension bridge across the Hàn River mouth.

text.description:
Thuận Phước Bridge is a suspension bridge that crosses the mouth of the Han River, where the river meets the sea. It is the longest suspension bridge in Vietnam: 1,850 metres long and 18 metres wide, with a main span of 405 metres and two towers 80 metres high. Building began in 2003 and the bridge was inaugurated on 19 July 2009. That scale is what makes it such a good subject. The long deck and tall towers give you strong lines to work with, and the river and sea sit in front and behind.

For a phone photo, the best view is from the water's edge rather than from the bridge itself. The riverside promenade along Đường Như Nguyệt, on the west bank upstream of the bridge, shows the bridge from below and across the river. After dark, the lit-up structure reflects on the water. If you want a close-up of the whole bridge rising over the river, the bridge's own walkways are an alternative, and the waterfront near Cảng Tiên Sa shows it with the river mouth, the bay and the green slopes of Sơn Trà behind. Whichever you choose, include some water in the frame, because the reflections and the sense of span depend on it. Keep the phone level so the deck does not appear to sag, and wipe the lens before you start.
text.geographic_location: In Da Nang, where the Han River meets the sea. The bridge links the two banks of the river mouth, close to the Tiên Sa port area and the green slopes of Sơn Trà.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops nearby, so go from central Da Nang to the Han River mouth by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the riverside park on Đường Như Nguyệt. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole bridge across the water. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and river, but keep the bridge in the middle of the frame so the edges do not stretch it. Use telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to pick out the towers and cables.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Đường Như Nguyệt (Riverside promenade along the west bank of the Han River, upstream of the bridge). The bridge seen from below and across the river, with the lit-up structure reflecting on the water at night. On the riverside promenade along the west bank, upstream of the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines and put the waterline on the lower third, so the reflection fills the bottom of the picture and the bridge runs across the upper part. Keep the towers upright by lining them up with the vertical grid lines. For a different view, try the bridge's own walkways or the waterfront near Cảng Tiên Sa, which adds the bay and Sơn Trà behind the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on a railing or wall to keep the phone still. Tap on the brightest part of the bridge and drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights do not turn into white blobs.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Night, when the bridge is lit up and reflects on the water. Sunset also works for a close-up from the bridge, though guides give different times for it, so arrive a little early.

text.access_note: The riverside promenade is a public park, but access to the port waterfront may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The bridge is lit up at night and its lights reflect on the Han River.
The riverside promenade on Đường Như Nguyệt is a free public park.
Access to the waterfront near Cảng Tiên Sa may be restricted.
The bridge's own pedestrian walkways are free and open, and the climb is slightly steep.
Sunset views of the bridge are good, with guides giving different times for sunset or the lit-up period.
Resting your elbows on a railing helps keep the phone steady for night shots.
